doc.title: Howard Levy interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 11, 2025

title: Piano lessons at Manhattan School and transposing in all keys
summary: Levy strayed from written pieces as a child, then discusses the Bird and George Shearing story and the importance of transposition.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: Did you have piano teachers who – did you stray from the compositions you were supposed to be playing during lessons and have piano teachers saying like, "What are you doing there? You can't do that.”

Oh yes. Because when I was a kid and studying at Manhattan School you know they had these student concerts. And so a lot of us would be assigned the same pieces. And you know I would hear the stuff that the other kids played. And I’d get to a passage in a piece that I’d heard before and go, “God, this is hard to read, I think it goes like this.” You know. So I would never play wrong notes, but I would be playing over the correct changes but I would you know, have my own little inner voicings, my own little melodies or something. And my teacher would go, “Wait a minute, it doesn’t sound wrong but that’s not Schubert” you know that kind of thing. It was exasperating to my teacher, yeah.
Yeah. Well the fact that you recognized the changes that Schubert was using I think is significant anyway.

Oh yeah. I mean I just had an innate sense of harmony. But you know everyone is born with certain abilities and then it’s just a matter of okay, if you’re going to try to get in the pond with the big boys, all right, it’s great that you can do this and you can do that, but can you play “All the Things You Are” in all twelve keys? In any tempo? I mean I know Bird kicked George Shearing’s ass one night. I heard that story. You know George Shearing came over from England and he’s sitting there at some club on 52nd Street and he thinks he’s, you know, the cat’s meow. And Bird says, “All right, I heard about you, you know get up, let’s play “All the Things You Are.” And he said, “In B minor.” It’s like [counts off fast]. You know. And George Shearing went home with his tail between his legs and said, “Okay, now I see the level of these guys.” Because this is what’s frightening is the level that these guys with big names, what their level actually was. And this is what the general public has no idea, the ability to transpose anything into any key at the drop of a hat. And this is something I work on a lot. And as a jazz pianist of course, who you know I did play a number of gigs accompanying singers and it’s like okay I want to play – this one singer used to do “Sophisticated Lady” in D. Okay? And so it’s like I had to play “Sophisticated Lady” in D. I mean no rehearsals. Like okay, “Sophisticated Lady” in D. It’s like okay. And your on-the-job training. It’s like how am I going to think about this? Am I thinking like relative? Like functional harmony of like now I’m going to the 2-5 of the 4 or am I just like doing this organically. This is one of the main things that jazz musicians can do that average musicians don’t know how to do is transpose. And I actually had training at that at Manhattan. They had us transpose things when I was studying classical piano. And even now I play Bach inventions, there’s

a few that I’ve played for my whole life, the number 4 [scats] that one. I transposed it into all twelve keys. And I do it with my eyes closed and you know, all that kind of stuff. Because there’s no cheating in music. I mean either you can or you can’t do it. And then I have to slow down. Okay I know what it sounds like but my fingering sucks when I’m playing it in F sharp minor. I’m like, “What’s the right fingering here?”
